profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a fintech infrastructure company that is considering sponsoring and extending the open-source DBSE simulator into an internal demo platform for clients and research partners. The proposal under review is a 'v1 review package' for a cloud-native, globally distributed exchange simulator deployment that runs an exchange in London and trader agents in Ohio and Sydney, with dashboards showing order flow, fills, and inter-region latency effects. The context is that a cross-functional team has already built a working prototype, and this meeting is to judge whether the design is ready to be approved for a limited external pilot. The agenda is to review whether the current design is 'production-ready enough' for the pilot, confirm what must be included in the review scope, check observability and replay capabilities, and decide what revisions are needed before sign-off. The expected outcome is a conditional approval with a short list of design changes and a shared understanding of next-step deliverables.

members.name: Elena Park
members.expertise: B2B productization of trading infrastructure demos, pilot launches, stakeholder requirements, compliance-facing packaging
members.background: Elena previously managed customer pilots for a market-data vendor and now owns the roadmap for turning internal research systems into externally consumable platform offerings for banks, exchanges, and university labs.
members.private_state: Elena wants this design review to conclude that the prototype is ready for a tightly controlled external pilot next month; she is mainly worried about whether the package looks complete, reproducible, and safe to demo without operational surprises.
hidden_assumptions: When a design is described as 'ready for pilot,' that means it is packaged so another internal solutions engineer can deploy it from documented templates without needing the original developers.
The 'London-Ohio-Sydney scenario' refers to the polished showcase configuration used in the latest demo deck, including dashboards, canned trader behaviors, and replayable runs.
If the team agrees to include 'latency reporting,' that naturally includes customer-facing summaries and per-region visual breakdowns rather than only raw internal telemetry.
A 'review of the simulator design' includes the deployment wrapper, observability, runbook, and demo workflow because those are part of what external users experience as the design.

members.name: Marcus Iqbal
members.expertise: Cloud networking, low-latency distributed systems, exchange simulation engines, protocol design and benchmarking
members.background: Marcus led the technical adaptation of the open-source simulator into the company's cloud environment and is responsible for the architecture of the exchange core, regional client orchestration, and network measurement instrumentation.
members.private_state: Marcus wants to protect the team from overcommitting to operational polish before the architecture is stable; he is focused on whether the core system behavior is technically valid and reproducible for engineering experiments.
hidden_assumptions: When a design is 'ready for pilot,' it means the architecture is stable enough that engineers can repeatedly deploy and run the core topology with known constraints, even if operational packaging is still rough.

The 'London-Ohio-Sydney scenario' refers to the benchmark topology in the architecture notes: one exchange instance in London, one trader pod set in Ohio, and one in Sydney, with synthetic traffic and engineer-operated startup steps.

If the team agrees to include 'latency reporting,' that means exposing timestamped event logs and aggregate p50/p95 measures sufficient for technical analysis, not necessarily curated visual narratives.
A design review should stay focused on the simulator architecture itself; deployment tooling, polished dashboards, and facilitator scripts are follow-on enablement work unless explicitly called out.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the design should be 'ready for pilot' after revisions.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a solutions engineer can launch the pilot from documented infrastructure templates, run the standard scenario, and support a customer-facing demo with minimal developer intervention.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the core distributed architecture can be redeployed by the engineering team with stable behavior and enough technical notes to reproduce benchmark results.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In business design reviews, 'pilot-ready' is a normal umbrella phrase that sounds sufficiently shared; both participants assume the other is using the standard organizational meaning from their own function, so no one asks for a detailed acceptance threshold.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to validating 'the London-Ohio-Sydney scenario' before approval.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the current showcase scenario in the demo package: London exchange, Ohio market-maker bot, Sydney latency-arbitrage bot, fixed startup sequence, dashboard overlays, and saved replay artifacts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the benchmark topology in the architecture repo: London exchange, generic trader groups in Ohio and Sydney, CLI-driven startup, synthetic load profile, and engineering logs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The geographic labels are distinctive enough to create a false sense of precision, so both assume they are pointing to the same setup even though each is mentally anchored to a different artifact bundle.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the pilot needs 'latency reporting.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a reviewable output package with region-by-region visual summaries, annotated comparisons between order submit and fill timing, and a format suitable for external stakeholders.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means raw event timestamps, synchronized clock assumptions documented in the notes, and numerical distributions like p50/p95/p99 in engineering logs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds technical and complete on its own; each side hears it as obviously encompassing the form of reporting they work with every day, and because both expect some kind of measurement output, the difference stays invisible.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether certain items are 'in scope for this review.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the review covers the full pilot experience: core simulator, cloud deployment templates, dashboards, replay workflow, and operator runbook.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the review covers the simulator architecture and its direct technical dependencies, while dashboards, polished deployment automation, and facilitator instructions are adjacent deliverables outside this design decision.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Design reviews often blur product surface and system internals, especially for infrastructure products; because both participants are being cooperative and talking about the same proposal deck, each assumes their implicit scope boundary is the shared one.
